extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, legislators, economists, and students of political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical criteria for financing, organizing, and regulating the administration of justice and public works (roads, bridges, canals, post-office, etc.), including who should pay, how charges should be structured, and how management/ownership affects incentives and corruption. Targets policy design and institutional arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of judicial presents/fees to prevent corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: When the people contribute by taxes it was commonly stipulated that no present for the administration of justice should, under any pretence, be accepted either by the sovereign, or by his bailiffs and substitutes, the judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abolishing presents was supposed easier than regulating them; prohibition of judicial presents aims to prevent corruption that naturally results from arbitrary and uncertain emoluments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed salaries for judges to replace ancient emoluments
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed salaries were appointed to the judges, which were supposed to compensate to them the loss of whatever might have been their share of the ancient emoluments of justice; as the taxes more than compensated to the sovereign the loss of his.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salaries paid by the crown are intended to remove judges' dependence on fees/presents, though practical salary levels and the continuing need to pay lawyers/attorneys mean litigation remains costly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence: separation from executive power
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial should be separated from the executive power, rendered as much as possible independent of that power. The judge should not be liable to be removed from his office according to the caprice of that power. The regular payment of his salary should not depend upon the good will... of that power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When united, justice is frequently sacrificed to politics; separation and independence preserve individuals' security and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid executive control of the fund that maintains the judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: It does not seem necessary that the person or persons entrusted with the executive power should be charged with the management of that fund, or with the payment of those salaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funds for judges might arise from rents or interest held by courts, but unstable funds are improper for permanent institutions; executive control risks politicizing judicial maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-pays tolls proportional to usage for infrastructure funding
rubrics_metrics.description: A highway, a bridge, a navigable canal, for example, may, in most cases, be both made and maintained by a small toll upon the carriages which make use of them... when the carriages pay toll in proportion to their weight or their tonnage, they pay for the maintenance exactly in proportion to the wear and tear which they occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an equitable method: tolls are advanced by carriers but ultimately borne by consumers; because such public works lower carriage costs, the consumer still gains overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build public works only where commerce requires them and to appropriate scale
rubrics_metrics.description: When high-roads, bridges, canals, etc. are in this manner made and supported by the commerce which is carried on by means of them, they can be made only where that commerce requires them... Their expense, too, their grandeur and magnificence, must be suited to what that commerce can afford to pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructing magnificent works where commerce is absent or for personal/political vanity. Scale and location should reflect genuine commercial demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate ownership/management depends on the work: private for canals, trustees for highways
rubrics_metrics.description: In several parts of Europe the toll or lock-duty upon a canal is the property of private persons, whose private interest obliges them to keep up the canal... The tolls for the maintenance of a highroad cannot, with any safety, be made the property of private persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private proprietorship can align incentives for canals (which become impassable if neglected), but high-roads can be neglected while tolls continue; trustees/commissioners with oversight are preferable for high-roads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require oversight and accountable management of toll trustees
rubrics_metrics.description: If mean and improper persons are frequently appointed trustees; and if proper courts of inspection and account have not yet been established for controlling their conduct, and for reducing the tolls to what is barely sufficient for executing the work to be done by them; the recency of the institution both accounts and apologizes for those defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turnpike abuses can be remedied by appointing proper trustees and establishing inspection and accounting mechanisms to prevent excessive levies and slovenly work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turning user-tolls into general revenue (regressive and economically damaging)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the tolls which are levied at the turnpikes should ever be considered as one of the resources for supplying the exigencies of the state, they would certainly be augmented... the turnpike tolls... instead of facilitating the inland commerce of the country, would soon become a very great incumbrance upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using tolls as a general revenue source encourages frequent augmentation, raising transport costs disproportionately on bulky goods and thus harming production and the poor (regressive because levied by weight not value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fee structures that incentivize verbosity or prolongation of proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been the custom in modern Europe to regulate, upon most occasions, the payment of the attorneys and clerks of court according to the number of pages which they had occasion to write... the attorneys and clerks have contrived to multiply words beyond all necessity, to the corruption of the law language of... every court of justice in Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment tied to pages/length encourages unnecessary prolixity; similarly, court revenue tied to number of proceedings can tempt multiplying processes—both corrupt legal efficiency and raise costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design fee distribution to reward diligence (pay after decision; proportion by effort)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the fees of court are precisely regulated and ascertained, where they are paid all at once, at a certain period of every process, into the hands of a cashier or receiver, to be by him distributed in certain known proportions among the different judges after the process is decided and not till it is decided... by proportioning the share of each judge to the number of hours and days which he had employed in examining the process... those fees might give some encouragement to the diligence of each particular judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting fees centrally and distributing them after resolution, proportionate to time worked, aligns incentives for timely, diligent adjudication and avoids perverse incentives to delay or scuttle work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer local/provincial revenue and administration for local works
rubrics_metrics.description: Even those public works, which are of such a nature that they cannot afford any revenue for maintaining themselves, but of which the conveniency is nearly confined to some particular place or district, are always better maintained by a local or provincial revenue, under the management of a local and provincial administration, than by the general revenue of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local administration ties benefits to payers and ensures attention to numerous small, useful works that a distant executive might neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use differentiated tolls to make luxury contribute more
rubrics_metrics.description: When the toll upon carriages of luxury, upon coaches, post-chaises, etc. is made somewhat higher in proportion to their weight, than upon carriages of necessary use, such as carts, waggons, etc. the indolence and vanity of the rich is made to contribute... to the relief of the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progressive or differentiated user charges can shift burden toward luxury consumption and ease the impact on essential goods transport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public institutions that are socially valuable but unprofitable require sovereign provision
rubrics_metrics.description: The third and last duty of the sovereign or commonwealth, is that of erecting and maintaining those public institutions and those public works, which though they may be in the highest degree advantageous to a great society, are, however, of such a nature, that the profit could never repay the expense to any individual, or small number of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes defense, administration of justice, works facilitating commerce, and institutions for instruction (education for youth and adults); these may require various degrees of expense across historical stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer stable funds for permanent institutions; avoid precarious endowments
rubrics_metrics.description: That fund might arise even from the interest of a sum of money, the lending out of which might, in the same manner, be entrusted to the court which was to be maintained by it. A part... arises from the interest of a sum of money. The necessary instability of such a fund seems, however, to render it an improper one for the maintenance of an institution which ought to last for ever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While rents or interest funds can supplement salaries, instability makes them unsuitable as the primary support for institutions intended to be permanent.
